paras: The lynching of Samuel Ramey was the hanging of a prisoner taken from the jail at Owingsville, Kentucky, by a band of masked men on the night of September 11, 1881. Ramey had been jailed for the killing of a young farmer, John Smith, a few days earlier. A brief Louisville wire carried the story to papers across the country within two days, and later Owingsville dispatches added that some thirty masked horsemen had done it.

According to the wire, Ramey had served a term in the penitentiary and was "a very hard case"; the Chicago Tribune called him a man with "a hard reputation." He was accused of killing Smith in Bath County, "four days ago" by one version of the dispatch. The Stanford Interior Journal, which named him "Samuel Ragland," said he shot Smith to death with a rifle and that "the killing was entirely unprovoked." An Owingsville dispatch of September 14 said he had been arrested in Rowan County and lodged in the Owingsville jail.

About midnight, a party of thirty-two horsemen rode into Owingsville, forcibly took Ramey from the jail and hanged him to a tree a short distance from town, according to the Wheeling Intelligencer's dispatch. An earlier Owingsville dispatch described the men as masked and numbered them at thirty-two in the New-York Tribune and thirty in the Alexandria Gazette. No report names any of the men or mentions the jailer.

No report of an inquest, an arrest of the lynchers, or any official response appears in the coverage. A week later, the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian noted only that Ramey had been taken from the Owingsville jail "last week and lynched by a mob."

The story reached most readers through a Louisville dispatch of September 12, which ran almost word for word in Chicago, Memphis, Los Angeles, Nevada and Minnesota papers. Headline writers gave it short tags such as "Lynched," "A Murderer Lynched," "Judge Lynch Again," "A Very Hard Case Hanged" and "Disposed of." Garbling in transmission produced versions placing the town in "Owensville" or "Dowingville," the state in "Me.," and the dateline in Leadville or St. Louis, spelling the victim's name as Ramsey, Ramsay, Romey, Romney, Karney, Raney or Rainey, and, in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union's copy, moving the hanging to "Saturday night."

Nearly every text treated Ramey's guilt as settled, calling him "the murderer of John Smith"; the Juniata Sentinel was the only paper found that described him as "accused." The Wheeling Intelligencer headed its dispatch "Informal Punishment by Night Riders," and two Ohio weeklies ran the story as "Mob Law in Kentucky." The Kentucky papers gave it a single line among state news, without comment on the mob. None of the reports mentions the race of Ramey, Smith or the lynchers.

Reports differ on the night of the hanging. The Louisville wire said "last night" on September 12, other briefs said Sunday night, and the Eaton Democrat said "the night of the 11th." An Owingsville dispatch of September 13 said "yesterday morning," which fits the later report that the horsemen came about midnight. Single briefs gave Monday night or "the 10th."

bases: Thirty or thirty-two masked men took a man held for murder from the Owingsville jail and hanged him (A6, A9, A18).

Ramey was forcibly taken from jail by a band of thirty or thirty-two masked horsemen and hanged, without any legal process, while held for the killing of John Smith (A6, A9, A18). Every report frames it as punishment for that killing (A4, A20).

A Louisville wire (A4), separate Owingsville dispatches (A9, A18) and two Kentucky papers (A20, A22) agree that he was taken from the Owingsville jail and hanged; they differ only on the night and the spelling of his name.

conflicts.note: A midnight hanging on the night of Sept. 11 reconciles the Sunday-night and Monday-morning versions; the Monday and 'the 10th' versions appear only in single briefs (one reprint of the wire, A12, also reads 'Saturday night').
Both figures come from Owingsville dispatches.
Ramey is the form in the Owingsville dispatches and the Hopkinsville paper; the rest look like telegraph and typesetting variants.
